author: Carlleyle
asr_identification: Bhuila (Bhuila Dih), Basti district; not Nagar Khas
evidence: Nagar Khas not visited personally; information from an exploring party sent there
quote: For, in order to be at all certain that I had really found Kapz/a-vasti, I had not only to identify the site of the city itself, but I had also to identify the sites of a number of other places … I however, in the meantime, sent a party of intelligent men to Nagar Khds, in order to explore the whole place
note: Against Cunningham's Nagar (Nagar Khas) of Ancient Geography (1871); Mizutani: Tilaurakot (Nepal).

author: Carlleyle
asr_identification: rejects Nagar Khas (Basti district); prefers Bhuila Dih
evidence: exploring party found no stupa near Nagar Khas; Chando Tal lake c. 3 miles long against Bhuila Tal c. 1.5 miles
quote: From the general conclusions that I drew from the above information which I received concerning Nagar Khas and its immediate neighbourhood, it appeared to me that it could not have been the site of Kapila-vastu
note: Rejects Cunningham's 1871 Nagar Khas (on second-hand information); the great mound perhaps one of the ten deserted towns. Mizutani: Tilaurakot.

author: Carlleyle
asr_identification: Bhuila (Bhuila Dih), Pargana Mansurnagar, Basti district
evidence: survey and explorations at Bhuila and neighbourhood; relies on Remusat/Laidlay's Fa-Hian for bearings
quote: I will now proceed to my more special report on the result of my actual investigations and explorations at Bhuzia, as my proposed site of Kapilavastu
note: Revises Cunningham 1871 (Nagar Khas), with Cunningham's guidance acknowledged. Mizutani: Tilaurakot; Bhuila Dih was later rejected (Rummindei/Nigali Sagar finds 1895-96).

author: Carlleyle
asr_identification: Bhuila Dih, Basti district, with its satellite sites
evidence: programme: identify the surrounding sites named by the pilgrims (Krakucchanda's and Kanakamuni's birthplaces, massacre stupas, arrow-well, Rohini, Lumbini, River of Oil, Koli)
quote: it was, as I have already intimated, also absolutely necessary that I should, at the same time, be able to discover and identify several other sites of interest at various distances from it, which were mentioned by the Chinese travellers Fa Hian and Huen Thsang
note: List of sites to be found; identifications in 337.

author: Carlleyle
name_in_asr: Kapilavastu; Sarakupa; birth-place of Kraku-chanda; birth-place of Kanaka muni
asr_identification: Bhuila Dih (Bhuila Tal, Pargana Mansurnagar, Basti district); Sarakupa = Sarkuhia 4.5 miles S; massacre stupas = Bhata/Kosihara 1.5 miles NW; Krakucchanda = Nagar (Khajura Nagara) 8 miles NW; Kanakamuni = Khopoa Dih near Kanakpur 6 miles W
evidence: distances and bearings from Bhuila measured on the Indian Atlas and on the ground
quote: Bhuila Dih, as Kapilavastu, situated on a Jake called Bhuil Tai in Parganah Mansiirnagar, in the District of Basti … The Sarakupa, at Sarkdhia, 44 miles to the south from Bhuila … The birth-place of Kanaka mimi, at Khopoa Dih, near Kanakpdr, 6 miles to the west from Bhuila.
note: Summary list of all Carlleyle's identifications. new: stupas of the massacre of the Sakyas (釋種誅死處) at Bhata/Kosihara. All differ from Mizutani (Tilaurakot, Nigali Sagar, etc.) and from Cunningham 1871 (Nagar Khas).

author: Carlleyle
note: Fort of Kot near Bhuila: description; at most one of the 'ten deserted towns'; no identification.

author: Carlleyle
asr_identification: Bhata (Kosahra), 1.5 miles NW of Bhuila Dih, half a mile NW of Sarnagi, Basti district
evidence: explored 8 miles NW of Bhuila; brick-strewn high ground with a grove; at Bhuila coins of Agnimitra (Sunga) and Indo-Scythian coins
quote: I have, however, explored the country for a distance of 8 miles to the northwest from Bhuzla and the only remains of any number of stiipas that I have been able to find, is at a site called “ Bhaté,’ or “ Kosahra,’’ about a mile and a half to the north-west from Bhuzla dih
note: new: stupas of the massacre of the Sakyas (釋種誅死處), NW of Kapilavastu; depends on Bhuila = Kapilavastu.

author: Carlleyle
asr_identification: Nagra (Nagar), NW of Bhuila, Basti district
evidence: discusses conflicting bearings in Julien's Hwen Thsang (south) and Beal/Remusat's Fa-Hian (SW vs NW); chooses Remusat
quote: the two Chinese travellers differ diametrically in their statements as to the position of the town in which Krakuchanda was born … but they differ entirely as to the direction, or the points of the compass.
note: Separates Krakucchanda's birthplace from Kshemavati (against Cunningham 1871, who cited the Sapta Buddha Stotra). Mizutani differs (Nepal Tarai).

author: Carlleyle
asr_identification: Nagra, 8 miles NW of Bhuila Tal, Basti district; Kshemavati = Khemrajpur (Pargana Amorha)
evidence: ancient village and ruin mound of Nagra with one standing stupa and remains of another; a mound S of the town by a tank; no trace of the name found; Kshemavati located at a mound near Khemrajpur
quote: while I belieye that I have, without doubt, discovered the birthplace of Krakuchanda, yet that I have not up to the present time been able to find any trace either of his name … I found the ancient village and mound of ruins of “ Magra,” with one stipa still existing, and the remains of another
note: Name etymologies (Nagar-Patijia, Napit Nagara). Differs from Mizutani and Cunningham 1871.

author: Carlleyle
asr_identification: Khopoa (Khopawa) Dih, three-quarters of a mile SSE of Kanakpur, 6 miles W of Bhuila, Basti district
evidence: large ruin mound on the N side of a lake; village name Kanakpur
quote: there isa-village called ‘Kanakapur’’ (the “Kunukpoor’’ of the maps); and only three-quarters of a mile to the southsouth-east from “ Kanakpur,”’ there is alarge ancient mound of ruins, called “Kopoa’’ or “Khopoa Dth,’’
note: Mizutani: Nigali Sagar pillar (Nepal). Rests on the village name only.

author: Carlleyle
name_in_asr: Lumbini Garden; River of Oil; Sara-kupa
asr_identification: Lumbini near Shiwpur, E of Bhuila; River of Oil = Bairahwa Nala, Gadi Nala and upper Majhora river; Sarakupa = Sarkuhiya 4-5 miles S of Bhuila (Basti district)
evidence: distance Sarkuhiya-Shiwpur measured on the map c. 6.5 miles, matching Cunningham's inference of 6-7 miles
quote: River of Oil,” on which the Lumbint Garden was situated, with the Bairahwa Nala, the Gadi Nala, and the upper part of the Majhéra river, close to the south of Shiwpur; and I have also other reasons for believing that the Lumbznz Garden was situated near Shiwpur.
note: Mizutani: Lumbini = Rummindei (Nepal; pillar found 1896).

author: Carlleyle
asr_identification: near Shiwpur, c. 7 miles E of Bhuila Dih, Basti district
evidence: distance Bhuila-Shiwpur 7 miles direct, 8 miles travelled; former sal forest at Shiwpur (claimed)
quote: The distance of Shiwpur from Bhuila Dzh (or Kapilavastu) is nearly 7 miles direct, but in travelling I myself found it to be fully 8 miles, which agrees, as nearly as possible, with the distance of the Lumbini Garden from Kapilavastu, as given by Fa-Hian.
note: Mizutani: Rummindei.

author: Carlleyle
asr_identification: Korau (Kuraon) Dih, 28 miles ESE of Bhuila Dih, Pargana Jhowlee, 11 miles SE of Basti town
evidence: great mound larger than Bhuila Dih, near Nagra and Bhagwanpur villages
quote: About half a mile to the south of BhagwAnpur, there is a village called Kuraon, or Korau, or Kurawa, which is situated at the eastern edge of a great mound of ruins, which is larger than the great Dih of Bhuila
note: Cunningham 1871: Deokali (28 miles E of Nagar). Mizutani: disputed (Ramagrama usually in the Nepal Tarai).

author: Carlleyle
asr_identification: Korau Dih, Basti district
evidence: town mound c. 2,100 x 1,400 ft; high brick stupa mound to its NW (Hwen Thsang's bearing taken as reversed); local ancient name Sobh-man-nagara
quote: It is this extensive mound at Korau that I believe to have been the site of the ancient town of Ramagrdma … The great mound of ruins at Korau measured about 2,100 feet in length from east to west; by about 1,400 feet in breadth from north to south.
note: Revises Cunningham 1871 (Deokali).

author: Carlleyle
asr_identification: Korau Dih, Basti district
evidence: sagar lake 1,700 ft E-W N of the town mound = the Naga tank; small mounds with lingams; tank = monastery site
quote: This lake, or sdgar, still remains pretty full of water, and I believe that it represents the tank, or lake of water, in which the Nagas lived who kept guard over the stipa
note: Footnote by Cunningham: he visited Koron-dih himself (account in ASR vol. XI).

author: Carlleyle
asr_identification: Maneya = Maniya (Mheneea) near the Khiduwa Nadi, 34 miles ESE of Bhuila; Ramagrama alternatively Wardi Dih (c. 20 miles direct from Bhuila)
evidence: measured map distances Wardi Dih-Maniya 15 miles; Deoram Ghat with a mound on the Kuano river 3 miles SW of Wardi Dih
quote: I have correctly identified the site of “Maneya” with a mound of ruins situated near a place the name of which is spelt ‘‘Mheneea” in the maps, but the real name of which is “ Maniya,” or‘ Mainiya,”
note: Wavers between Korau Dih and Wardi Dih for Ramagrama. Cunningham 1871: Anoma = Aumi river.

author: Carlleyle
asr_identification: Chandbhani (Chund baree), E bank of the Ami river, 12 miles ENE of Korau Dih, 7.5 miles NE of Maneya
evidence: name likeness; map distances
quote: I would, therefore, be inclined to identify the site of the Chandaka-nirvatana stdpa with a place called “ Chandbhani,” the “Chund baree” of the maps, which is situated on the east bank of the Ami river, 12 miles direct to the east-north-east from Korau Dih
note: Cunningham 1871: Chandaoli on the Aumi, 10 miles S of Gorakhpur.

author: Carlleyle
asr_identification: 3-5 miles NW of Sahankat (near Rudrpur), not Sahankat itself
evidence: computed road distances from Chudrao or Judean
quote: General Cunningham has identified the ruins of an ancient city named “ Sahankat,” somewhere about a mile and a half to the north-west of ‘ Rudrpur,” as the site of the city of the Moriyas, who built the “ashes stiipa.” But the distance is too great for the ‘ashes stipa,”
note: Shifts Cunningham 1871 (Sahankat) a few miles NW; no site found.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: mound of China (Chine), 11 miles from Amritsar
evidence: visited the lofty mound
quote: Passing through Lahore I visited the lofty mound of China, 11 miles from Amritsar, which, I have no doubt, is the Chinapati of Hwen Thsang, which Kanishka made the winter residence of the Chinese hostages.
note: Preface. Revises Ancient Geography 1871 (Patti); agrees with Mizutani (Chiniyari).

author: Cunningham
name_in_asr: Asoka's stupa N of the Body-gift stupa; monastery of the wicked Yaksha
asr_identification: Asoka's stupa = Ventura's great tope at Manikyala (bearing read south for north); Yaksha monastery = Mera, 9 miles E of the Manikyala tope
evidence: dome top 91 ft above ground; oblong mound E of the stupa = monastery; Mera thup turned out a Muslim tomb of re-used stones; vihara No. 5 excavated (110 x 52.5 ft) with two copper coins of Kanishka
quote: I think it almost certain that the bearing should be “ south,” which would identify Asoka’s stipa with the great Manikydla tope opened by Ventura … the very exact agreement of. both bearing and distance from Manikydla are strongly in favour of Mera being the position of the monastery and sttipa of the wicked Yaksha
note: Built on Body-gift = Court's tope (AG 1871); Mizutani places the body-gift site in Buner (Banj), not Manikyala.

author: Cunningham
note: Colossal figures at Mahal, Manikyala: Hwen Thsang's account called meagre; no location argued.

author: Cunningham
name_in_asr: stupa where Buddha pricked his body (blood-offering)
asr_identification: stupa opened by Ventura near Rama-ka-Pind, c. 24-25 miles S of Court's tope at Manikyala
evidence: Rama mound = monastery; red soil and thorns as in the pilgrim's account; Balesar Pind nearby with burnt wood and a coin of Syalapati Deva
quote: which I think may be identified with that which Hwen Thsang mentions as standing on the site where Buddha had pricked his body with a bambu spike to nourish a starving tiger with his blood.
note: new: stupa of the blood offering (刺身出血), S of the body-gift stupa. Mizutani places the body-gift site in Buner.

author: Cunningham
name_in_asr: stupa of Kunala; place of the head-offering
asr_identification: Kunala stupa = site of a great stupa on the terrace at the N foot of the Meri hill, E of the old town of Taxila; the 80 small stupas there perhaps part of the 1,000 stupas of the head-offering
evidence: excavated c. 80 small votive stupas (empty) on a rocky platform; squared stones on an upper terrace; plinth of a small building 15 ft 9 in
quote: The position lies to the east of the old town, and seems to me to correspond very well with the site of the great stipa which was built on the spot where Kunala, the son of Asoka, had his eyes put out
note: Bearing E instead of SE admitted. Mizutani: Kunala on the Hathial ridge (Marshall); head-offering = Bhallar stupa. AG 1871 had the head-offering in Babar-khana.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: fort of Chine (near Amritsar)
evidence: local rhyme on the bricks of the fort
quote: Thus of the fort of Chiné the Chinapate of Hwen Thsang, in which Kanishka kept the Chinese hostages, it is said
note: Passing mention; see 361.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Bhera on the Jhelam
note: Faxian-only place (Pi-cha = Bhera); not in the Xiyu ji.

author: Cunningham
note: Bhera history (Mahmud); footnote to Beal's Fa Hian only.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: great mound near Ransi, 9 miles S of Shekohpura, c. 25 miles W of Lahor
evidence: survey of the mound: small fort upwards of 150 ft square with a broad ditch
quote: Between Sangalawdla and Lahor, close to the village of Ransi, there is a great mound of ruins, which I feel confident represents the ancient town of Narasinha.
note: new: Narasiṃha (那羅僧訶城) between Śākala and Cīnabhukti; first proposed in ASR II.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Manikyala: the great stupa opened by General Court, 200 li SE of Taxila (ruined city near Shah-dheri)
evidence: inscription in Court's deposit mentions the Huta-muria 'body-offering' twice; Sung-yun's 3 days SE
quote: The scene of this legend is placed by Hwen Thsang at 200 Jt, or nearly 34 miles to the south-east of Taxila, which is the exact bearmg and distance of M4nikyala from the ruined _ city near Shah-dheri.
note: Same as AG 1871 (Sin-tu read as Suhan). Mizutani: Banj mountain, Buner.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Chine (Chiniyari, Chine-ka-theh): villages Unchakila, Bichlakila and Shahbazpur, 11 miles from Amritsar on the road to Parsarur and Sialkot
evidence: survey: central mound 400 ft square, 46.5-50 ft high, with a lower mound of double size on N and NE; large bricks 12.5 x 8.5 x 2.5 in; Mirza Mughal Beg's 'Chiniyari, also called Alexander's mound'
quote: As the position of Chiné, or Chiniyari, agrees most exactly with that of Chzndpatz, as laid down by Hwen Thsang, I have no doubt as to the correctness of this identification … I made a survey of the place, and found the central mound to be 400 feet square and from 46} to 50 feet in height.
note: Revises Ancient Geography 1871 (Patti); agrees with Mizutani (Chiniyari).; 04.02.03 removed (passage is about Chine only)

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Sultanpur (Dalla Sultanpur), left bank of the Kali-Veni, 24 miles WSW of Jalandhar
evidence: black mud quagmire round the town (seen 1846) as the origin of 'black forest'
quote: Its position corresponds almost exactly with that of the great monastery of Za-mo-su-fa-na or Témasa-vana, the “black forest,” which Hwen Thsang places 25 miles to the south-west of Jalandhar.
note: AG 1871 named no site; agrees with Mizutani (Sultanpur, citing Cunningham).

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Sultanpur: the Badshahi serai on the old mound
evidence: serai 485 ft square, walls c. 15° out of the meridian (suspected monastery foundations); mound 30 ft high; old mounds of large bricks over the town
quote: I have a strong suspicion, therefore, that the walls of the serai. must ‘have been built on the foundations of the old Buddhist monastery

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Sultanpur
evidence: bricks 11.5 x 8 x 2 in; carved brick, female figure, clay mould of Ganesa; no seals
quote: I have no doubt, however, that deeper excavations would bring to light many of these relics, and perhaps also some of the ‘‘teeth and bones” of the Buddhist saints alluded to by Hwen Thsang.
note: Followed by Dalla (not a Xiyu ji place).

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Rajaori
quote: In the same way the Rajapura of ihe Raja Tarangini and of Hwen Thsang has now become Rajaori.
note: Passing remark (in the Panchapura inscription discussion); agrees with AG 1871 and Mizutani.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Kurukshetra round Thanesar, 200 li (5 yojanas) on each side
quote: this name is certainly as old as the 7th century, as Hwen Thsang calls it “le champ du bonheur.’? In his time the extent of the chakra was 200 47, or 5 yojanas
note: Reads 200 li as on each side (circuit 20 yojanas) = Samantapanchaka.

author: Cunningham
note: Kurukshetra boundaries from the Mahabharata and Manu; Hwen Thsang only in a footnote.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Asthipur, W of Thanesar
evidence: no bones visible now
quote: The site where the dead bodies of the slain are said to have been burned is now known by the name of Asthzpur, or the “ place of bones.” - It was seen by Hwen Thsang in A.D. 635
note: Xuanzang's heaped bones of Kurukshetra located at Asthipur.

author: Cunningham
note: Later history of Thanesar.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Asthipura (Madrasa Tila), W of Thanesar, S of Aujas Ghat
evidence: excavations in the mound (700 x 500 ft): platform of unbaked bricks 364 ft long, walls, terracottas, burnt stone fragments, head of Siva
quote: Bones of large size were still to be seen here in the time of Hwen Thsang … 1 made several excavations in this mound, which brought to light an extensive platform of unbaked bricks still 364 feet in length

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Rajaori
quote: The earliest mention of Rajaord is by Hwen Thsang, who came from Kashmir by way of Ko-lo-che-pu-lo, or Rajapuri to the plains of the Punjab.
note: History from the Rajatarangini; agrees with AG 1871 and Mizutani.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: country of the Kunindas; capital Sugh near Buriya, W bank of the Jumna
evidence: coins of Amoghabhuti, king of the Kunindas, found most plentifully in this district
quote: so the country of the Kaunindas has been described by the pilgrim under the name of Srughna. Now the capital of Srughna I have already identified with Sugh, near Buriya
note: New argument: Srughna = Kuninda country; AG 1871 and Mizutani: Sugh.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Sugh and neighbourhood
evidence: Kuninda coins (silver hemidrachms, copper) found in greatest numbers about Sugh
quote: I have further identified it with the Srughna of Hwen Thsang, as the coins bearing the name of the Kunindas are found in greater numbers about Sugh and its neighbourhood than in any other part of the country.

author: Cunningham
note: Index.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Gunamati = Dharawat ruins N of the Barabar hills (Kunwa hill); Buddha's mountain = Barabar hill; peak over Silabhadra's monastery = Kauwa Dol
evidence: discoveries at Dharawat; name of the Kunwa hill
quote: I think there can be no doubt that the Dhardwat ruins are the remains of the monastery of Gunamati, which Hwen Thsang visited on his way from Pataliputra to Gaya. This identification is rendered absolutely certain by the very exact correspondence of the Barabar Hill, and the Kauwa Dol Peak
note: Preface. Revises AG 1871 (Gunamati near Nidhi on the Pewar; Silabhadra = Bithawa hill). Mizutani gives no identification for either monastery; Barabar = 08.04.02 agrees.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Mahasthan on the Karatoya river (Bogra); Po-shi-po = Bhasu Bihar 4 miles W
evidence: distance and bearing from Rajmahal; Bhasu Bihar village name
quote: I was fortunate enough to discover the site of the ancient city in Mahasthan on the Karatoya River. The proof of the identification rests partly on the agreement of the distance and bearing from the neighbourhood of Rajmahal, and partly on the immediate vicinity“ of Bhdsu Bihar
note: Preface. Revises AG 1871 (Pubna); agrees with Mizutani (Mahasthan, Vasu-Bihar).

author: Cunningham
name_in_asr: Kukkuta-pada-giri; Kapotika Sangharama (Pigeon Monastery); temple of Avalokiteswara
asr_identification: Cock's Foot hill = three peaks of the Murali hill 3 miles NNE of Kurkihar (Gaya district); Pigeon Monastery = Parbati, 10 miles NE of Giryek, 11 miles SE of Bihar
evidence: Murali hill: square basement on the middle peak, bricks 17x10x3 and 12x10x3 in; monastery mound Sugatghar c. 120 ft square; 37 figures and ten inscriptions (c. 800-1000) at Kurkihar. Parbati: hill 1,750 x 1,000 ft covered with ruins in terraces; mound G (400 ft square) with wedge-shaped stupa bricks on its E side; dargah on site A
quote: I am now satisfied that Parbati was the place actually visited by the pilgrim … But as the place is also called Ghar Pérdvat, or the ‘ Pigeon’s House,’ I think there can be no doubt whatever that it is the “ Pigeon Monastery” of Hwen Thsang.
note: Kurkihar confirms ASR I (AG 1871 and Mizutani similar). Parbati revises AG 1871 (Bihar, reading 60 li) and differs from Mizutani (Bihar Sharif) and Broadley (Bihar hill).

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Parbati hill (Bihar)
evidence: excavated mound D: basement 18.5 ft square with stumps of 16 granite pillars, stucco mouldings; lac seal; clay lump with four impressions of a Gupta-period monastic seal ending sanghasa (Rodaksha Sanghasa?)
quote: The word sanghasa at the end is, however, quite distinct, so that there can be no doubt. that the seal belonged to one of the Buddhist sanghas of PArbati.
note: Seal shows a Buddhist sangha at Parbati; does not name Kapotaka.

author: Cunningham
name_in_asr: monastery 40 li SE of the Pigeon Monastery
asr_identification: Aphsar (conical mound), reading 4 li for 40
evidence: no remains at 40 li; Aphsar has Buddhist and Brahmanical remains, boar statue; Gupta inscription found there by Kittoe
quote: In the position indicated there are no remains of any kind. It seems probable therefore that we should read 4 & instead of 40, which would take us to the high conicamound of Aphsar
note: Revises AG 1871 (Titarawa). Mizutani: no settled identification.

author: Cunningham
name_in_asr: large village south of the Ganges; Lo-in-ni-lo
asr_identification: large village = Shekhpura (Kali-math-pokhar tank); Lo-in-ni-lo = Rajjana (Rajjaona), 2 miles NW of Lakhi-Sarai station on the Kiyul
evidence: bearing and distance; subsequent route 'through forests and gorges'; Mathokar Tal
quote: I feel sure therefore, that the large Brahmanical village visited by Hwen Thsang must have been situated in the pretty and wellwooded oasis of Shekhpura.
note: Revises AG 1871 (near Daryapur; Rohinila). Shekhpura agrees with Mizutani (Shekhpur, emending the distance); Mizutani leaves Lo-in-ni-lo open.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Rajjana, W bank of the Kiyul near Lakhi-Sarai (Mongir district)
evidence: route-book distance Balguzar-Mongir 30.5 miles (pilgrim 200 li); Balguzar Jhil = the great lake N of the stupa; northern mounds with Buddha and Padmapani statues (monastery and stupa)
quote: Iconclude, therefore, with some confidence, that Rajjdna is the true representative of the Lo-22-nz-lo of Hwen Thsang.
note: Revises AG 1871 (Rohinila, after Vivien). Mizutani: unsettled.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Mongir hill (Kashta-harana Parvata)
evidence: local name Harana Parvata from the Kashta-harana Ghat; legends
quote: Now, this name of Harana-Parvata is clearly the original of Hwen Thsang’s /-/an-na-Po-fa-to, which Julien has rendered by Hiranya Parvata or the “Hill of Gold.”
note: New etymology (Harana, not Hiranya); location as AG 1871 and Mizutani.

author: Cunningham
name_in_asr: double-peaked hill of the Yaksha Vakula
asr_identification: Mahadeva hill and the hot springs of Bhimband, 11 miles from the Kiyul, W frontier of Mongir district
evidence: two-peaked isolated hill; hot springs on its N side flowing into the Mon river (Buchanan's description)
quote: This place I would identify with the hill of MahAdeva and the hot springs of Bhimband, which are situated only 11 miles from the Kiyul River, on the western frontier of the Mongir district.
note: Mizutani: Uren hill, 20 miles SW of Monghyr. Not in AG 1871.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Bhimband
evidence: cut stones carried off to Kharakpur; Panch Kumar figures gone; springs the hottest in the district
quote: Nothing in fact now remains save the two peaked isolated hills and the hot springs, which are the hottest in the district, thus agreeing with Hwen Thsang’s description of them as being “extremely hot.”
note: Followed by Singi Rikhi (not a Xiyu ji place).

author: Cunningham
note: Sultanganj vihara: quoted account says Hwen Thsang gives no clue to it; no identification.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Mayaganj cave at Bhagalpur
evidence: long rock-cut gallery; punch-marked silver coins found in it
quote: A similarly remote age is claimed by Hwen Thsang for a long gallery at this very place, regarding which he gives the following legend
note: new: the cowherd's cave/gallery near Campā (牧牛人石室) not in the table. Champa = Bhagalpur as AG 1871 and Mizutani.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Kahalgaon (Colgong) rocks, 23 miles E of Bhagalpur; cave = Mayaganj cave
evidence: three rocky islets; old channel Marganga; brick temple ruins on the summit with sandstone jambs, bricks; small rock-cut temple below the summit
quote: Both bearing and distance point to the rocky hill of Kahalgaon (Kolgong of the maps), which is just 23 miles to the east of Bhagalpur.
note: Revises AG 1871 (rocky island opposite Patharghata, 24 miles E). new = herdsman's cave (see 386).

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: capital near Rajmahal; district named Kankjol (16 miles S of Rajmahal)
evidence: Pilgrim's 400 li E of Champa; name theories (gali 'pass'; Kajoli sugarcane)
quote: According to HwenThsang’s distance from Champa or Bhdgalpur, the capital should rather be looked for in the neighbourhood of Rajmahal.
note: As AG 1871 (Rajmahal district named after Kankjol) and Mizutani (Rajmahal = Kankjol).

author: Cunningham
name_in_asr: Kajangala capital; high tower on the Ganges
asr_identification: capital possibly Kankjol (c. 70 miles from Bhagalpur through the hills); tower = Teliyagarhi (Teliya-gali); Paundravardhana capital = Mahasthan
evidence: walls and towers of Teliyagarhi built in alternate courses of stone and brick; Buddhist and Brahmanical statues once there
quote: I am led to think that this tower was most probably situated at Teliya-garhi itself.
note: Tower (大臺) not identified by Mizutani or AG 1871.

author: Cunningham
note: Gauda history (Jayapida, Pala chronology).

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Bhasu Bihar, 4 miles W of Mahasthan (Bogra district)
evidence: great brick stupa mound 30 ft high W of the village; temple ruin of carved brick to its N; Sosong Dighi tank
quote: But I did not hear of Bhésu Bihér until my arrival at Bihar itself, when the name at once struck me as being the very one intended by the pilgrim’s Po-shi-fo.
note: Agrees with Mizutani (Vasu-Bihar).

author: Cunningham
name_in_asr: Po-shi-po monastery, stupa and vihara of Avalokiteswara
asr_identification: monastery = Bihar mound (700 x 600 ft); stupa = Bhasu Bihar mound; vihara = ruined temple N of the stupa
evidence: Bihar mound with trenches of dug-out walls, bricks 11x6x3 in; temple 13 x 11 ft inside, walls 4 ft, enclosure 104 x 64 ft, carved bricks
quote: The great monastery I would identify with the mound of Bihar itself, which is 700 feet by 600 feet broad.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Mahasthan, 100 miles E of Rajmahal (Bogra)
evidence: survey of the fortified city 4,500 x 3,000 ft, with suburbs c. 7,000 x 4,500 ft (under 4.5 miles circuit) against 30 li; local tradition as capital of Barendra; pan gardens; rejects Westmacott's Bardhan Kuti
quote: This city the pilgrim places at 600 /7, or 100 miles, to the east of the Ganges, near Rajmahal. Now this description corresponds exactly with the relative positions of Rajmahal and Mahdsthan, the latter being just 100 miles to the east.of the former.
note: Revises AG 1871 (Pubna); agrees with Mizutani.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Mahasthan, in the district of Silbaras (Bogra)
evidence: Brahmanical remains at Mahasthan; district name Silbaras read as Silavarsha 'moist district'
quote: Hwen Thsang notices that the country was low and moist, and this leads me to suggest that the name of the district of S7/baras,in which Mahasthan is situated, must be Sz/avarsha, or the “ wet or moist district.”

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Bagdi: the delta between the Jalinghi and the Megna (Bikrampur chief town)
quote: It corresponds with the district called Samatata by Hwen Thsang, and by Samudra Gupta in his Allahabad pillar inscription.
note: Region as AG 1871 (Gangetic delta); no capital named. Mizutani: capital Bad-Kamta (disputed).

author: Cunningham
note: Pala history; Hwen Thsang's silence on a ruler.

author: Cunningham
note: Chronology (Amsuvarman, Aditya Sena).

author: Cunningham
note: Maukhari chronology; Purnavarman.

author: Cunningham
note: Chronological table.

author: Cunningham
note: Index.

author: Cunningham
name_in_asr: promenade along which Buddha took exercise
asr_identification: Bodh Gaya: raised promenade just outside the N wall of the Mahabodhi temple
evidence: promenade found almost intact during the clearance; two rows of stone pillar bases, each marked with a letter of the Asoka alphabet (vowels on the S row, consonants on the N), showing a covered walk (cankramana)
quote: One of the most intereggng discoveries was that of the raised promenade, along which Buddha was said to have taken exercise. This was found almost intact just outside the northern wall of the present temple.
note: Preface. new: Buddha's promenade (佛經行處) N of the Mahābodhi temple not in the table.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Kunwa hill at Dharawat (Gaya district)
evidence: excavations on the Kunwa hill: stupa with every brick stamped with a stupa; deposit of 520 cowries and two clay seals in Gupta letters (Buddha; Tathagatasya Buddhasya). Also excavations at Besarh (Vaisali) and at Bakhra near the Monkey tank
quote: At the last I made several excavations on the Kunwa hill, which was beyond all doubt the site of the Gunamati monastery described by Hwen Thsang.
note: Preface. Revises AG 1871 (near Nidawat on the Pewar). Mizutani gives no identification.

author: Cunningham
note: Change of the Gandak's course inferred from the pilgrim's crossing only the Ganges from the Drona stupa to Vaisali; no place located.

author: Cunningham
name_in_asr: old city where the Licchavis took leave of Buddha
asr_identification: Kesariya, 30 miles NW of Vaisali
quote: which he had given to the Licchavis when they took leave of him at the old city on their northern frontier, which I have identified with Kesariya, 30 miles to the north-west of Vaisali.
note: Passing mention in the alms-bowl history; as AG 1871 and Mizutani.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Besarh (Vaisali)
evidence: excavations across the ramparts: only broken bricks; clay whorls, copper trenail, beads, cast copper coin; burnt-clay inkstand with Gupta inscription Sri Vidasatya
quote: Of the existing remains at Vaisali I have already given an account in my former report. During my late visit I made a few excavations across the ramparts, in the hope of finding some portion of the old walls.
note: Mostly on Buddha's alms-bowl (Fa-Hian). Location as AG 1871 and Mizutani.

author: Cunningham
name_in_asr: lion pillar of Asoka and the monkey tank
asr_identification: Bakhra (Kolhua), 2 miles NW of Besarh: lion pillar, tank and stupa
evidence: pillar measured: total 45 ft 3 in above water level (shaft 35 ft 10 in, capital with lion 9 ft 5 in); stupa N of the tank 20 ft high, 75 ft diameter, bricks 13.5 x 9.5 x 2.5 in; tank 240 x 140 ft; mound 1,000 x 600 ft
quote: In my former Report on Vaisali? I have identified the lion pillar and tank of Bakhra with the lion pillar of Asoka and the monkey tank to the south of it, which were seen by Hwen Thsang to the north-west of the city of Vaisali.
note: Agrees with Mizutani (Kolhua pillar). Tank = Markata-hrada.

author: Cunningham
name_in_asr: stupa of the monkey's honey offering
asr_identification: small brick stupa at the W end of an excavated wall, W of the monkey tank, Bakhra
evidence: excavation: small stupa (7-8 ft diameter) with ornamented bricks and a circular umbrella brick; probably only votive; Buddha statue found in 1854 720 ft N of the pillar
quote: In the position occupied by this small stipa, Hwen Thsang places the stipa which marked the spot where the monkey offered Buddha a pot-full of honey. I can scarcely suppose that the small stipa which was found in the excavation was the monkey’s honey-offering stdpa
note: new: monkey's honey-offering stupa (獼猴奉蜜窣堵波) W of the tank, not in the table.

author: Cunningham
name_in_asr: ancient town deserted for ages (Mahadeva's birthplace)
asr_identification: Kesariya, 28-30 miles NW of Besarh, E of the Gandak
evidence: great stupa called Deora of Raja Ben Chakravartti; crossing of two high roads; Raja Ben-ka Digha (3,000 ft) as Buddha's 'great stream'
quote: It therefore corresponds exactly with the position of Hwen Thsang’s ancient town, which had been deserted for ages, and of Fa-Hian’s site, where the Licchavis of Vaisli took leave of Buddha.
note: As AG 1871 and Mizutani.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Gunamati = Buddhist remains at Dharawat (Beglar's identification); mountain = Barabar peak; Teladhaka = Tillara
evidence: route measured from Teladhaka: 90 li SW to Barabar, 30 li NW to Dharawat
quote: The Buddhist remains at Dhardwat have been identified by Mr. Beglar with the Gunamati monastery of Hwen Thsang … Both the bearing and the distance point to the famous peak of the Barabar Mountain
note: Adopts Beglar; revises AG 1871 (mountain between Giryek and Gaya; Gunamati near Nidawat). Barabar agrees with Mizutani; Mizutani has no site for Gunamati.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Dharawat (Kunwa hill), Gaya district
evidence: stupa on the hill with clay seals in Gupta characters (4th c. or earlier); two small temples (7 ft 9 in and 5 ft square) with nine unburnt clay seals of the creed (9th-10th c.); punch-marked silver coin
quote: I think it probable that this stipa on the hill above must be coeval with the foundation of the monastery below, and that both must be referred to the time of Gunamati.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Kauwa-dol hill, 17 miles NNE of Gaya, 2 miles W of the Barabar caves
evidence: stupa-shaped granite peak c. 500 ft high; mounds with bricks and pottery near Shamspur at the N foot; carved granite blocks; Brahmanical rock reliefs
quote: Kauwa-dol has been identified by Mr. Beglar with the site of the Silabhadra Monastery of Hwen Thsang, an assignment with which I fully concur.
note: Adopts Beglar; revises AG 1871 (Bithawa hill). Mizutani gives no identification.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Kauwa-dol, near Shamspur (Samaspur)
evidence: 14 granite pillars 7 ft high in groups before a colossal Buddha; remains over 97 x 67 ft; foundation of a long E-W wall; standing figure with the creed (9th-10th c.)
quote: I take these pillars to be the remains of the great monastery of Silabhadra, which Hwen Thsang describes as being situated near an isolated hill.

author: Garrick
asr_identification: Besarh (Besadh), with the Raja Bisal-ka-garh fort
evidence: desultory excavations at Besarh; fort mound c. 6 ft high with moat and traces of brick ramparts
quote: The village of BesArh, or BesAdh as it is commonly called by the people, has been identified by General Cunningham with the ancient Buddhistical site described by Huen Thsang, the Chinese pilgrim, under the name of Vazséii
note: Garrick's report (ASR XVI part 2). As AG 1871 and Mizutani.

author: Garrick
asr_identification: Kasia: Matha-Kuar-ka-kot mound
evidence: mound c. 250 paces NW-SE; ruined circular brick mass with a conical brick tower (votive stupa built over another)
quote: The site of Kasia has also been identified with that of Ausznagara, or “Town of the Kusa-grass,” which, as the scene of Buddha’s death, was famous throughout the Buddhistical history of India.
note: As AG 1871; Mizutani follows the common view (disputed).

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: colossal Nirvana statue at Kasia (Matha-Kuar)
evidence: statue (discovered by Carlleyle) with an inscription of the Gupta period; Garrick's description of the restored figure and pedestal
quote: As this colossal statue representing the Nirvana of Buddha bears an inscription of the Gupta period, it must be the identical figure that was seen and described by the Chinese pilgrim Hwen Thsang. The statue was discovered by Mr. Carlleyle.
note: Cunningham's footnote to Garrick's report. Agrees with Mizutani.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Devisthan or Ramabhar Tila mound, Kasia
evidence: Garrick: mound of solid brick dug by an earlier explorer (well 10 ft wide, 50 ft deep, three trenches); earthen pot of black seals reported
quote: General Cunningham is of opinion that this mound might possibly be’the famous cremation stipa of Buddha, mentioned bythe Chinese pilgrim Hwen Thsang.
note: Garrick reporting Cunningham's view (AG 1871: Devisthan). Mizutani: cremation site c. 10 miles E (or should be W).

author: Garrick
asr_identification: Khukhundo (Khukuno), E Gorakhpur district
evidence: numerous Brahmanical sculptures; countless small brick mounds; brick-digging in an oblong mound SW of the village
quote: The site rendered celebrated by the chronicles of the Chinese pilgrim Hwen Thsang, who records that Here lived a wealthy Brahman devoted to Buddhism.
note: Garrick follows the Khukhundo identification; AG 1871 preferred Kahaon. Mizutani gives no identification.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Maha-Kosala = Chhattisgarh, extended W over Vakataka (Chanda, Nagpur, Seoni) to make up 6,000 li
quote: At the time of Hwen Thsang’s visit in A.D. 639 he describes the kingdom as 6,000 /, or 1,000 miles, in circuit, an extent which could have been attained by inclusion of the great district of Vakataka
note: Revises AG 1871 (Vidarbha/Berar, capital Chanda): now Chhattisgarh plus Vakataka. Closer to Mizutani's recent view (upper Mahanadi).

author: Cunningham
note: Dynastic history of Maha-Kosala (Hwen Thsang's Buddhist Kshatriya king; So-to-po-ho = Satavahana).

author: Cunningham
note: Dynastic history; few Buddhist traces in Chhattisgarh.

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: not Asni (Fatehpur district); Ayodhya = Pi-so-kia (Visakha)
evidence: visit to Asni: no Buddhist remains; old fort and a mound c. 200 ft square on the Ganges with bricks 12 x 8.5 x 2 in
quote: I was induced to visit Asni in the hope that it might turn out to be the old Buddhist site described by Hwen Thsang under the name of O-yu-to, which M. Julien has rendered by Ayodhya.
note: Asni rejected for lack of Buddhist remains. AG 1871: O-yu-to = Kakupur. Mizutani prefers Führer's Aphui (Fatehpur region).

author: Cunningham
name_in_asr: monastery of Upagupta; cave of bambu spikes; dry tank of the monkey
asr_identification: Mathura: city = the Kattra; Upagupta monastery = the fort on the Jumna, 1 mile E; cave mountain = Ambarikha mound; monkey tank = tank by the Collector's kacheri mound (Jalalpur)
evidence: survey of the fort and mounds: high grounds of Hansganj and Sital-ghati taken as the pilgrim's 'mountains', hollows as 'valleys'; distances Ambarikha-kacheri tank 3.5-4 miles; Huvishka-period pillar bases and Buddha figures from the kacheri mound
quote: If, then, we accept the Kattra asthe site of the ancient city, the Sangharama, or monastery of Upagupta, which was situated on a mountain, one mile to the east, will be exactly represented by the present fort.
note: new: dry tank where the monkey fell (獼猴池), SE of Upagupta's cave. Mizutani: Upagupta's monastery cannot now be located.

author: Cunningham
note: Savara tribes; passing mention of Kirna-Suvarna (Varaha Mihira's Sauri-Kirnas).

author: Cunningham
asr_identification: Kasia: great stupa and the Nirvana statue on its W side
evidence: Carlleyle's excavation of the Nirvana statue, 20 ft long, lying on the right side facing W, with a Gupta-period inscription; vaulted temple
quote: By his patient and methodical explorations at Kasia) Mr. Carlleyle has fixed its identification beyond all doubt. On the west side of the great Stipa he discovered the famous Nirvana statue of Buddha, just as it was described by the Chinese pilgrim Hwen Thsang.
note: Preface. Cunningham also accepts Carlleyle's Kapilavastu (Bhuila) as the western 'fixed point', abandoning his own Nagar Khas of AG 1871.

author: Carlleyle
asr_identification: Rampur Deoriya, near the head of the Marawa Tal (Gorakhpur district)
evidence: ruined brick stupa c. 20-25 ft high between two ancient tanks, 500 ft NE of the village; village on a ruin mound; brick platform at the NW corner (monastery?); six tanks, five ancient
quote: This, then, is the Rdmégrdéma of the Buddhist chronicles … from the result of my own discoveries, it is evident that Hwen Thsang must have meant to say either that the stipa was situated to the north-east of the town
note: Revises Carlleyle's own Korau Dih (ASR XII) and Cunningham's Deokali (AG 1871). Mizutani: disputed.

author: Carlleyle
asr_identification: Rampur Deoriya; the Naga tank = the Marawa Tal lake
evidence: stupa 2,000 ft W of the Marawa Tal (lake c. 1.5 miles long); old river bed from the lake to the Katnaya
quote: But, having thus now finally and conclusively identified Rémpur Deortya with Rémdgrdéma, it may be asked how it was that in my report on Bhuila, or Kapilavastu, | had proposed to identify Koraon ath, about 3 miles’ further to the south, with Rémdgrdma ?
note: Explicit retraction of Korau Dih (ASR XII).

author: Carlleyle
asr_identification: Rampur Deoriya, c. 26 miles SE of Bhuila
evidence: map distances; Koli/Vyaghrapura = Barah Chhetra (Varaha Kshetra) 9 miles E of Bhuila; Sarakupa = Sarkuhiya
quote: I also rémembered, at the same time, that General Cunningham had himself estimated the probable distance of Ramdgrdma from Kapilavastu at about 28 miles.
note: Koli (Faxian/Pali, not Xiyu ji) put at Barah Chhetra.

author: Carlleyle
asr_identification: Rampur Deoriya
evidence: travelling distance Bhuila-Barah Chhetra-Rampur c. 30 miles against 200 li; local report of a deori (conical brick mound)
quote: Thus, in every single particular, s—in name, in distance, in position, and in the possession of a stupa, and a.mound of ruins,—Rémpur agrees or coincides exactly with Rémégrama

author: Carlleyle
asr_identification: Anoma = Kudawa nadi ('river of the leap'), 1 mile NE of the ruins at Tameswar Nath (Maneya)
evidence: measured route Rampur-Tameswar Nath 12 miles (9.5 direct); total Bhuila-Kudawa nadi 43 miles = Lalitavistara's 6 yojanas
quote: Now, I have identified the Anoma river with the Aiédawd nadz, which literally means “the leaped river,” or “the river of the leap.”
note: AG 1871: Anoma = Aumi river.

author: Carlleyle
name_in_asr: three stupas (Chandaka's return, cut hair, changed garments)
asr_identification: beyond (E of) the Anoma, near the Sirsarao Tal
evidence: Hwen Thsang's 100 li read as measured to the three stupas; 10.5 miles direct, c. 15 miles travelled from Rampur Deoriya
quote: the distance given by him of “too &,” or 162rds miles, eastwards, from Rémdgrdma, was not calculated to the Anoma river, but to the three stipas just mentioned

author: Carlleyle
name_in_asr: three stupas; stupa of the cut hair
asr_identification: high ground E of the Sirsara (Sirsarao) Tal, 1 mile N of Lachmipur, 3.5 miles NE of Tameswar Nath, 2.5 miles SW of Maghar
evidence: village of Sirsarao on a mound; earthen conical stupa mound c. 10 ft high 400 ft E of the village; lake name read as Sirasarovar 'lake of the head'
quote: the spot which 1 have identified as the site of the three Stipas, is situated on some high ground, on the east side of a lake called the Sarsara, Sirsara or Sirsarao Tél, and about a mile or less to the north of a village called Lachmipur
note: Revises his own Chandbhani (ASR XII) and AG 1871 (Chandaoli/Chureya/Kaseyar).

author: Carlleyle
asr_identification: solid brick mound 300 ft NE of the Sirsara stupa mound; Maha-than mound 370 ft further N
evidence: brick mound c. 50 ft across, 5-6 ft high, formerly in a grove of jamun and jambu trees (Hwen Thsang's jambu tree); Maha-than round mound c. 100 ft across with ancient bricks
quote: It would therefore appear probable that this mound of solid brick may be the remains of the stipa which marked the spot where this change of dress took place.

author: Carlleyle
asr_identification: Rajdhani or Upadhaolia ruins on the Gorra river, 14 miles SSE of Gorakhpur, c. 30 miles SE of the Kudawa nadi
evidence: ruins extend c. 4 miles from the Rapti to the Pharend river, 1-1.5 miles broad; ruined area at the three stupas 1,400 x 700-800 ft
quote: I have identified the site of the city ‘of the Aforzyas with a very extensive series of ruins called Réjdhdud or Updhaolra, which are situated on the Gorra river, in the Gorakhpur district
note: Revises AG 1871 (Sahankat near Rudrapur) and Carlleyle's ASR XII placement NW of Sahankat.

author: Carlleyle
name_in_asr: City of the Moriyas in the Nyagrodha forest
asr_identification: Rajdhani-Upadhaolia
evidence: old bar (banyan) trees and Bar-names (Barhei, Barehi, Barhaira); map distance Kudawa nadi-Dih Ghat 30 miles
quote: The distance from the Kddawé nadi (which [ have identified with the Anoma), near Zameswar, to the tuins near Dih Ghét, is exactly 30 miles

author: Carlleyle
asr_identification: ruined stupa at the SE corner of the Great Dih, S of Gunsara (Rajdhani)
evidence: hemispherical solid brick stupa, 17-18 ft high, c. 75 ft diameter; mound at Baswi perhaps Asoka's 100-ft stupa
quote: I think that this ruined stdpa might possibly be identiflable with the famous Ashes Stépa of the City of the Mortyas

author: Carlleyle
name_in_asr: large town of the hospitable Brahman
asr_identification: Rudrapur (Sahankot/Nath-nagar), or the ruins near Baraon and Samogar 6 miles S of it
evidence: Kasya-Baraon 32 miles direct on the straight line to Benares; Rapti ghats used by pilgrims; forest between Rajdhani and Kasia
quote: I have identified either Rudrapur,—or else some ruins situated near Baraon and Samogar, about 6 miles to the south of it,—with the large town mentioned by Hwen Thsang, where a hospitable Brahman lived who was devoted to Buddhism … whereas, on the other hand, Khiékundo and Kahaon, which General Cunningham proposed, are respectively 11 miles and 14 miles too far east
note: Rejects Cunningham's Khukhundo/Kahaon (AG 1871). Mizutani gives no identification.

author: Carlleyle
name_in_asr: large city of the rich Brahman
asr_identification: Rudrapur
evidence: c. 25 isolated mounds, nearly all Brahmanical lingam temples; only four look like stupas
quote: This I believe to be the city, the “large city,” mentioned by Hwen Thsang, in which a rick Brahman lived, who was devoted to Buddhism, and where there were a number of Brakmanical temples.
note: Letter of May 1876 to Cunningham, quoted.

author: Carlleyle
asr_identification: Bar forest beginning 5 miles N of Rudrapur and extending to Mithabel and towards Rajdhani
evidence: forest wholly of bar trees
quote: and this must, therefore, be the “ Vyagrodha forest” mentioned by Hwen Thsang.
note: Supports Rajdhani over Rudrapur (Cunningham's Sahankat).

author: Carlleyle
asr_identification: Mithabel, on a ruin mound 7.5-8 miles N of Rudrapur, at the N edge of the Bar forest
evidence: double-topped brick mound (twin stupas?) and three or four dome-shaped mounds in the forest; statues of Narayan and Lakshmi
quote: and this thust, therefore, be the remains of the ancient Nyagrodha forest mentioned by Hwen Thsang

author: Carlleyle
asr_identification: Kasia: oblong mound W of the great stupa (Matha-Kuar-ka-kot)
evidence: shaft sunk 10 ft; uncovered a colossal recumbent statue on a broken throne in a chamber c. 30 x 12 ft, lying on the right side facing W, much broken
quote: as I was actually in search of the great Buddhist temple containing the famous colossal statue of the Nirvéna of Buddha mentioned by Hwen Thsang, it struck me that I might possibly have the good fortune here to hit upon some remains of the famous statue.
note: Discovery of the Nirvana statue (1876). Agrees with Mizutani.

author: Carlleyle
name_in_asr: Nirvana temple, great stupa and stone pillar
asr_identification: Kasia: temple and great stupa
evidence: ancient well 60 ft W of the temple; searched round the stupa for the inscribed pillar without result; stupa bricks measured
quote: I searched everywhere for this pillar in the course of my excavations, but I could not find any trace of it.

author: Carlleyle
asr_identification: Kasia great stupa
evidence: reconstructed height c. 177 ft (with umbrella perhaps 200 ft) from the pilasters of the circular neck; prefers c. 150 ft
quote: we shall then get an approximate total original height for the entire stiipa, of about 177 feet, which is somewhat below the estimate of Hwen Thsang

author: Carlleyle
asr_identification: ancient circular brick base 8 ft below the plinth, SW of the Kasia temple
evidence: circular base c. 15 ft diameter on a buried pavement, overridden by a medieval wall and a concrete floor
quote: Whether the ancient circular base which rests on this pavement be that of one of the many stipas mentioned by Hwen Thsang, I am not prepared to decide
note: Probably older than Xuanzang's visit (Carlleyle).

author: Carlleyle
asr_identification: small stupa base NNE of the great stupa; detached mound E of it
evidence: circular base 3 ft 6 in diameter 13 ft 6 in NNE of the great stupa's basement; stepped brick platform on the E mound
quote: This might possibly be the remains of one of the smallest of the lesser stipas mentioned by Hwen Thsang.

author: Carlleyle
asr_identification: detached mound E of the great stupa at Kasia
evidence: mound c. 50 ft diameter, 16 ft high, stepped brick on an earthen core; small unexcavated mound 150 ft S of the temple; Cunningham's mounds D, E, F since levelled
quote: I strongly suspect that the stone “ pillar” or “column” mentioned by Hwen Thsang must have stood on the top of this detached eastern mound
note: Inscribed pillar at the Nirvana stupa (not separately in the table).

author: Carlleyle
asr_identification: Subhadra's stupa possibly the Nat-ka-Than mound in the Khanua Nala, c. 2,000 ft W of Anirudhwa; cremation = great stupa of Ramabhar
evidence: Nat-ka-Than mound 180 x 19 ft (sic) in the channel; distances and bearings from the black Buddha statue; most outlying mounds ploughed away
quote: with the exception of the great stipa of Rdmabhdr, and the stipa of the Virvdna on the Mdathd-Kunwar-ka-Kot, | could not find any traces whatever of any other large stipa anywhere in or near the locality which embraces the site of the ancient city of Kustnagara.
note: new: stupa of Subhadra's nirvana (善賢入寂滅處) and other Kusinagara stupas not in the table. Cunningham's footnote corrects Carlleyle's bearing.

author: Carlleyle
name_in_asr: Deer stupa; relic-division stupa; cremation stupa
asr_identification: Deer stupa = small grassy mound near the Khanua Nala; relic division perhaps at the Ramabhar stupa; cremation at the Mallas' coronation hall
evidence: Ramabhar stupa of huge square bricks, Asokan age
quote: This great ruined stipa is certainly of great antiquity, and must be at least as old as the time of Asoka, judging by the great size and thickness of the IN 1875-76 AND 1876-77.
note: new: deer stupa (鹿王救兔) and relic-division stupa (八王分舍利) not in the table. Questions Ramabhar as the cremation stupa (AG 1871: Devisthan/Ramabhar).

author: Carlleyle
asr_identification: city proper = mound near Anirudhwa village; monastic city to its NW with the Nirvana temple
evidence: traced circuit c. 9,500-9,600 ft (under 1.75 miles) against 12 li; boundary ridges of the NW religious quarter
quote: This is about a quarter of a mile less than the estimate of Hwen Thsang, who says that the site of the ancient city had a circuit of about 12 Chinese /, which is equivalent to about 2 English miles.
note: Kasia as AG 1871; Mizutani follows the common view.
